opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what's mostly missing is serious thinking about what happens *after* the alignment problem is, in some sense, solved. A lot of the expert conversation is focused on the scenario where an AI system goes rogue: it has goals we didn't intend, it deceives us, it seizes power. That's a real concern and I'm glad people work on it. But there's a quieter scenario that I think gets much less attention, which is what my co-authors and I have been calling gradual disempowerment.

The basic idea is this. Right now, our civilization is aligned with human interests to a surprising degree, and not mainly because everyone is nice. It's because states, firms, and cultures all *need* humans. Governments need citizens to pay taxes and staff the army, so they have to keep people reasonably happy. Companies need workers and consumers. Even culture is produced by people for people. Those dependencies are an implicit bargaining position humans have had throughout history.

Once AI is competitive with humans at basically everything, that dependency starts to dissolve. A state that gets most of its revenue from AI-run industry doesn't need to care as much what its citizens think. A firm that can replace its workforce will, because competitors will. And none of that requires any single AI to be misaligned or any villain to be in charge. Each actor is just responding sensibly to competitive pressure, and the systems we've built gradually stop being steered by human needs.

What strikes me is that most of the expert analysis I see treats "the economy" and "the government" as if they'll keep working for us by default, and the only question is whether the AI is obedient. But obedience to whom? If every institution is optimizing for growth or power and humans are just a cost center, you can have perfectly obedient AIs and still end up with a world that has very little room for people.

So the gap, as I see it, is that we don't have good frameworks for thinking about civilizational alignment, about how to keep the big systems we live inside responsive to human values once humans stop being economically and militarily necessary. Economists, political scientists, and AI safety researchers each have a piece of it, but very few people are looking at the whole picture. And frankly, I don't think anyone has a convincing plan yet, myself included. That's a big part of why I wanted to talk about it.

r001.rationale: The response calls for better frameworks for civilizational alignment and says several fields have pieces of the problem. It does not present its analysis as deliberately amateur or as a way to provoke outside experts to respond.

r002.rationale: The response accepts AI competitiveness across domains as a premise and focuses on gradual disempowerment. It does not identify experts’ reluctance to contemplate that possibility as a major gap.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the thing that's most missing is that almost nobody is actually sitting down and asking: okay, suppose this goes well, suppose we get AI that can do everything humans can do, cheaper and better — what does the world look like after that? What happens to people?

There's a huge amount of expert effort going into forecasting when it'll happen, and into the alignment problem, which is basically making sure the systems do what we want. And those are important. But there's this strange gap where people say "transformative AI" and then just sort of stop, as if the transformation itself doesn't need to be described. It's like we're all staring at a cliff edge and debating how far away it is, without really talking about what's at the bottom.

And when you do try to think it through, the picture is kind of unsettling even in the case where alignment works. Right now, humans are economically and militarily necessary. Governments need us to pay taxes and fight wars, companies need us to work, and that necessity is a big part of why our interests get taken into account. Democracy and labour rights and so on didn't fall out of the sky — they came partly from the fact that states needed cooperative, educated populations. If AI can do all the work, that bargaining position just evaporates. You'd have a world where humans are, economically speaking, dead weight, and our continued wellbeing depends entirely on whoever controls the systems choosing to keep caring about us.

That's not a "the AI kills everyone" scenario. It's more of a slow, boring disempowerment, where institutions gradually stop being accountable to people because they no longer have to be. And I think that's underexplored precisely because it's not a dramatic technical failure — there's no single bug to fix. It's a question about what equilibrium the world settles into, and I don't think the expert analysis has really grappled with how to make that equilibrium a good one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses an underexplored social outcome, but does not present its analysis as deliberately amateur or as a prompt for experts outside computer science to offer better analyses.

r002.rationale: It says experts rarely consider what happens after AI can do everything humans can do, but does not identify reluctance to contemplate that level of machine capability itself as a major gap.

astra-6.text:
I think one thing that’s often missing is an account of what happens after that point. We tend to frame the question as, “When will AI be able to do all the things a human can do?” But that’s not necessarily a stable endpoint. If it can do research, including research on how to build better AI systems, then we have to ask how quickly that feeds back into further progress.

And being competitive with a human at a task isn’t the same as having the economic impact of one human. You might be able to run many copies, have them work continuously, and share improvements across them. So even without assuming some dramatic leap in intelligence, you could be looking at a very dramatic change in the amount of intellectual work getting done.

I’d like to see more analysis that makes those assumptions explicit. What’s holding progress back at that stage? Is it compute, experiments, access to the physical world, or something else? Those details matter enormously for whether we have decades to adapt or a much shorter period.

r001.rationale: The candidate asks for more explicit analysis of post-human-competitive progress and its constraints. It does not present deliberately amateur analysis as a way to provoke experts outside computer science.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies missing analysis of what happens after AI can do human tasks, but does not say experts are reluctant to contemplate AI becoming competitive with humans in every domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one thing that’s missing is a clear picture of what happens when these systems can do AI research themselves. We tend to talk about progress as though it’s driven by a fixed number of human researchers, with AI gradually making them more productive. But if you can make another copy of a very good AI researcher, then the amount of effort going into improving AI could change enormously.

That doesn’t establish that there’ll be an instantaneous intelligence explosion. There could be bottlenecks in experiments, compute, or getting useful ideas to work. But I’d like to see those bottlenecks made explicit. Which parts of AI research actually require a human? How quickly could you scale the other parts? And how much better would the resulting systems be at doing the next round of research? That feedback loop seems central to understanding what happens around human-level capabilities.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls for clearer analysis of AI research feedback loops, but does not present amateur analysis as a way to prompt experts outside computer science to improve their analyses.

r002.rationale: The candidate identifies missing analysis of AI systems doing AI research as the gap; it does not identify experts’ reluctance to consider machines competitive with humans in every domain.
